Dependency injection is one sentence: an object is given what it needs instead of building it. What it needs is a

, anything the class calls out to but doesn't compute itself: a clock, a logger, a database. Injected, that dependency arrives as a constructor parameter, a setter, or a parameter of the method that uses it; left uninjected, the class names a concrete type inside its own body and builds it there.

The problem is that a class which builds its own dependency can only be tested through whatever that dependency really does. A watchdog reading the system clock inside its own logic can only be tested by waiting: to see it fire, sleep past its timeout. Some questions survive no amount of sleeping, such as what a test should see when the clock stands still or jumps backward. The trouble isn't that the class is hard to test. It's that the one part worth testing has no handle a test can move.

How it works is that the dependency is named as an interface the depending class owns, not a concrete class from whichever library implements it, and that interface is a constructor parameter and a member, so the object is never in a state where the dependency is missing. A test then builds the object with a fake implementing the same interface: a fake clock the test moves by hand instead of a real one it has to wait on, a fake logger recording lines in a vector instead of printing them.

What it costs is a decision about where the dependency lives and how long it must survive: a reference member can't be null but needs the caller to keep the real object alive at least as long, and a class needing far more dependencies than a test can reasonably fake usually does too many things, not a case for bundling them into one parameter struct. Injection is also the wrong tool for a member that never varies, or a pure function, whose arguments already are its dependencies.

You meet this the moment a robot's node has to be tested off the real clock and outside a ROS graph, and it's the interview question itself: take a class that builds its own logger, change it so the logger is passed in, and write a test against a fake that proves what it logged.

subs.title: Constructor injection; depending on interfaces, not concrete classes

No amount of sleeping hits that. What happens when the clock jumps backwards, which simulation time does at the end of every

names the three places a dependency can enter an object, and the differences between them decide the design.

items.v: Constructor injection: the dependency is a constructor parameter and a member. The object is complete the moment it exists, the member can be
, and there is no state in which the dependency is missing.

function, called after construction. The signature of the class does not change, which makes it the cheap way into code you inherited, and Muldoon points out that the setter is often never called in production. The price is a window between the constructor and the setter where the member is empty, so every use has to check, and nothing stops a caller from swapping the dependency halfway through a run.
Method injection: the dependency is a parameter of the function that uses it. No member, no lifetime question, and the signature of every call changes.

c.v: Constructor injection is the default. Take the other two when something blocks it: setter injection for a class you cannot change the construction of yet, method injection when the caller already holds the value. The ROS 2 time topic used method injection for exactly that reason: a subscription callback already knows what time it is, so
takes the time per call rather than holding a clock. A watchdog driven by its own timer has no such caller, so it holds a clock.
What you inject matters as much as where.
is declared next to the monitor, by the code that needs logging. Klaus Iglberger's
CppCon 2020 talk on the SOLID principles

is built on this point: the Dependency Inversion Principle is satisfied only when the abstraction belongs to the high-level code. An interface that ships with the logging library, and grows whenever that library grows, leaves you depending on the library through one more hop. His book, C++ Software Design, makes the same argument as Guideline 9, on the ownership of abstractions. Guideline 4, design for testability, takes it one step further: its answer to "how do I test this private member function" is that the function is a separate concern in disguise, and that pulling it into a class of its own is both the design fix and the test fix.
Four ways to hold the injected dependency come up, and the failure cases section measures what each costs.

items.v: A reference or a raw pointer to an interface: the caller owns the object and guarantees it outlives yours (Core Guidelines
, which say a raw pointer or reference is non-owning). A reference cannot be null and cannot be reseated; a pointer allows both, which is what setter injection needs.
to an interface: your object owns the dependency, and the caller decides the concrete type. This is what a factory hands back, which the Factory Method topic picks up.
A callable held by value, usually
: the dependency is one operation rather than a set of them, and the object stays copyable.
A template parameter: the type is fixed where the object is built, there is no indirect call, and the whole class moves into a header.

c.v: Two cases are not dependency injection and should not be turned into it. A member the class owns outright and that never varies, such as the

a buffer keeps, is an implementation detail; injecting it publishes a decision nobody wants to make. And a pure function needs nothing injected, because its arguments already are its dependencies. Bilal Gill's
CppCon 2023 talk on testable ROS 2 code
pushes as much of a node as possible into that shape first, and injects only what is left: the clock, the transport and the log.

c.v: Start with what each way of holding a dependency costs in bytes. Each struct below holds one clock and one 8-byte timeout:

Speed follows the same split, and the gap is small. A template call is an ordinary call the compiler can inline; a call through
is an indirect call it can inline only when it can prove the dynamic type; a

call is an indirect call it can almost never prove. Here is the loop that measures it. The clock keeps the index and advances it on every call, so each call depends on the one before and the compiler cannot vectorise any version away:

head.v: Best of eleven, 50 million calls, over 16 runs of the program

c.v: The two indirect forms share a row because the measurement does not separate them. Their ranges overlap here, and the gap between them is not stable anywhere: in the Strategy topic's version of this benchmark, changing how the loop added up its result, which is work outside the call and is not timed differently, was enough to swap which of the two came out ahead. Treat them as one thing. On this machine, an Intel Core i7-14700HX with GCC 13.3, a call the compiler cannot inline costs roughly 0.4 to 0.9 ns more than one it can, counting both this measurement and the Strategy topic's. Put that where it belongs: a control loop reading the clock at 1 kHz pays under a microsecond a second for either.
Three warnings come with the number. These are at

, and every example on this page builds unoptimised with sanitizers, where all the rows are slower and the gap between them changes. They are one machine in one session: the same binary run while the machine had other work on it put the first row at 20 to 22 ms rather than 13 to 16. And a benchmark of this shape is delicate: an earlier version of this loop let the compiler fold the inlined row to a constant and reported a difference that was not there. Core Guidelines
is the rule to apply before letting any of this decide a design. Inbal Levi's
CppCon 2019 talk on virtual dispatch and its alternatives
benchmarks these against each other properly, and finds the ranking moves with the compiler and the optimisation level.
So why is the interface ever right? Because the template version moves the decision to compile time, and everything that follows from that is a cost:
. Without the concept the same mistake produces a wall of errors from inside
, so a template dependency needs a concept the way a virtual one needs a base class; Core Guidelines
asks for constraints on every template argument. Even with the concept, four costs stay.
is a template, so its definition lives in a header and every user recompiles when it changes. Its type now carries the clock, so whatever holds a

becomes a template too, which Muldoon's slide calls templates all the way down. The clock cannot be chosen from a ROS parameter at start-up, because the choice happens at compile time. And a dependency that crosses a shared library boundary, such as a plugin, cannot be a template argument at all.

Take a template parameter when the type is known where the object is built, the call is on a hot path, and you own the whole call chain. Take an interface when the choice is made at run time, the dependency crosses a binary boundary, or you are adding tests to code you cannot turn into templates. Muldoon's list of drawbacks for interfaces is honest about the other side: the interface accumulates functions, a fake has to stub out every pure virtual one even when the test touches two, and every call pays the indirect hop.
The second failure is about lifetime. A non-owning
is a promise by the caller, and nothing in the type system checks it:
on the read of the vptr inside
. The fix is a decision, not a cast: either the monitor owns the logger through a

, or the owner is declared before the monitor in the same class so that destruction, which runs in reverse, takes the monitor down first. Setter injection makes this worse, because the member has to be a pointer that starts null, and every use needs a check that a reference member would have made unnecessary.
The last failure is the one that turns up in real code. Injection makes dependencies visible, and a class with eight of them says so:

blocks.text:
Processor(Database& db, Transport& com, FileLoader& loader, Calculator& calc,
          Cache& cache, Clock& clock, Logger& log, const Config& config);

c.v: holding all eight, passed as one parameter. Muldoon's slide on that reads NOPE: an unstructured bucket moves the problem somewhere else and now every test has to fill a bucket. A struct of coupled data of simple types is fine; a struct whose job is to shorten a parameter list is not. Eight dependencies is a measurement, and what it measures is that the class does eight things. Split it, and each piece takes the one or two it needs. That is the same reading Iglberger gives a hard-to-test private member function in Guideline 4, and the same reason Core Guidelines

refuse the other escape route, which is to stop passing the dependency and reach for a global or a singleton instead. A singleton is a dependency that does not appear in any signature, and it is the third of the roadblocks Muldoon lists, after construction hidden inside a function and a class that gives you no handle to inject anything through.
